article.title: The Congo: A Land Cursed by Wealth
article.citation: Dan Snow, The Congo: A Land Cursed by Wealth, BBC News Website, 2013
paragraphs: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is often described as a paradox—a nation with the natural wealth to become one of the richest countries on earth, yet ranked among the poorest. Its history is a grim story of exploitation, violence, and corruption, shaped by centuries of colonialism and foreign interference.

The DRC has endured the world’s deadliest conflict since 1945, with more than five million people killed and millions more suffering displacement, disease, violence and famine. This devastating reality, sometimes called “Africa’s Great War,” has been fought largely within Congo’s borders, fueled by the fight to control its immense resources.

Ironically, it is these resources that lie at the heart of the country’s suffering. From the Portuguese slave trade of the 15th century to King Leopold of Belgium’s rubber empire in the 19th century, foreign powers have plundered Congo’s people and land. Millions died as men were enslaved to tap rubber, their families held hostage, resistance punished by mutilation and murder. Later, Congo’s copper, uranium, and coltan helped fuel world wars and the digital revolution—yet the Congolese themselves remained impoverished and uneducated, denied the chance to build stable institutions.

Independence in 1960 brought hope, but no preparation. With no trained elite to govern, chaos followed. The Cold War further destabilized the nation, with Western powers propping up dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, who looted billions while his people starved. His fall in 1997 triggered another brutal war, drawing in nine nations and countless militias. Today, Congo remains fractured. Its minerals still flow abroad, enriching elites and global industries, while its people endure poverty and instability. The Congo’s tragedy is not its weakness but its wealth—a blessing turned into a curse by centuries of exploitation.

languageFocus.title: Language Focus
languageFocus.instructions: Examine the key academic structures and discourse patterns used in Source B. Notice how the author constructs paradoxes, traces historical cause and effect, uses passive voice, and maintains source attribution.
languageFocus.topic: Paradox, Cause-and-Effect, Passive Voice, and Historical Sequencing
languageFocus.explanation: Historical current-affairs writing relies on precise language patterns to contrast potential with reality, explain multi-century causal chains, describe historical subjection without sensationalism, and attribute interpretations to source authors.

patterns.name: Paradox and Contrast Structures
patterns.explanation: Contrasts two coexisting, contradictory facts to emphasize an unexpected or tragic reality ('a nation with ... yet ranked among ...', 'not its weakness but its wealth').
patterns.example: The coastal province has the farmland to feed a nation, yet remains dependent on grain imports.
patterns.sourceExample: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is often described as a paradox—a nation with the natural wealth to become one of the richest countries on earth, yet ranked among the poorest.

patterns.name: Cause-and-Effect Relationships
patterns.explanation: Shows how economic incentives and resource competition directly trigger armed conflicts and institutional breakdown ('fueled by...', 'helped fuel...', 'triggered...').
patterns.example: The rapid discovery of offshore gas fields fueled intense maritime border disputes.
patterns.sourceExample: fueled by the fight to control its immense resources... helped fuel world wars and the digital revolution... His fall in 1997 triggered another brutal war...

patterns.name: Passive Voice and Past Subjection
patterns.explanation: Places the emphasis on the affected people and territories who suffered exploitation, rather than glorifying the perpetrators ('were enslaved', 'held hostage', 'denied the chance').
patterns.example: Local miners were forced into dangerous shafts and denied protective equipment.
patterns.sourceExample: Millions died as men were enslaved to tap rubber, their families held hostage, resistance punished by mutilation and murder.

patterns.name: Participle Clauses for Economic & Political Impact
patterns.explanation: Uses present and past participles to pack background causes and ongoing consequences into compact clauses ('shaped by...', 'drawing in...', 'enriching elites').
patterns.example: The newly built canal altered shipping routes, enriching port cities while bypassing inland markets.
patterns.sourceExample: shaped by centuries of colonialism and foreign interference... drawing in nine nations and countless militias... enriching elites and global industries...

patterns.name: Chronological Sequence Markers
patterns.explanation: Guides the reader chronologically through centuries of historical development ('since 1945', 'From the 15th century to the 19th century', 'Later', 'In 1960', 'In 1997', 'Today').
patterns.example: From early colonial trading posts in the 1600s to modern container terminals, the harbor expanded continuously.
patterns.sourceExample: From the Portuguese slave trade of the 15th century to King Leopold of Belgium’s rubber empire in the 19th century... Independence in 1960 brought hope... Today, Congo remains fractured.

patterns.name: Metaphor and Appositive Framing
patterns.explanation: Uses appositive phrases and metaphorical noun phrases to crystallize complex historical evaluations ('a blessing turned into a curse').
patterns.example: The nation's petroleum boom proved to be a fleeting triumph—a windfall squandered by inadequate oversight.
patterns.sourceExample: The Congo’s tragedy is not its weakness but its wealth—a blessing turned into a curse by centuries of exploitation.

sections.heading: Distinguishing Directly Stated Facts, Historical Sequences, Interpretations, and Inferences
sections.explanation: When evaluating historical informational texts, mature readers differentiate between empirical facts reported by the author, chronological historical sequences, the author's overarching analytical framing, and their own broader inferences.
examples: Directly Stated Fact: The DRC endured conflict claiming more than five million lives since 1945.
Chronological Sequence: Foreign exploitation moved from the Portuguese slave trade (15th century) to Belgian rubber extraction (19th century) and modern mineral mining.
Author's Interpretation: Congo's fundamental tragedy is its wealth rather than weakness, which external actors turned into a curse.
Student Inference: Sustainable peace in resource-rich nations requires transparent domestic institutions and accountable global supply chains.

sections.heading: Using Cautious Attribution Language
sections.explanation: When summarizing historical claims from a single source, use attribution tags such as 'According to Source B,' 'Dan Snow argues,' or 'the article suggests.' This demonstrates academic caution by crediting the specific author rather than presenting one text as the definitive historical absolute.
examples: Attributed Reporting: 'According to Source B, Western powers destabilized the DRC during the Cold War by supporting Mobutu Sese Seko.'
Attributed Framing: 'Dan Snow frames Congo’s paradox as a blessing turned into a curse through centuries of exploitation.'

writingPractice.title: Writing Practice
writingPractice.instructions: Complete these four targeted sentence-level writing activities. Write complete, grammatically sound sentences based on the evidence and language patterns in Source B.

writingTask.title: Final Writing Task
writingTask.instructions: Write a well-structured evidence-based historical explanation paragraph answering the prompt below. Follow the checklist and adhere strictly to the word count target.
writingTask.prompt: How does Source B explain why Congo’s wealth became a curse? Write an evidence-based historical explanation paragraph of 100–140 words. Use at least three accurate details from the source, include one historical sequence or cause-and-effect relationship, and explain the final contrast between weakness and wealth.
checklist: clear controlling idea answering how wealth became a curse
at least three accurate details from the original source
one historical sequence or cause-and-effect relationship
one source-reporting phrase such as 'According to Source B' or 'the author argues'
accurate use of contrast language such as 'yet', 'while', 'but' or 'not ... but ...'
explanation of the final wealth metaphor ('a blessing turned into a curse')
no invented statistics, current facts, political opinions or graphic details
the source’s viewpoint is presented as a viewpoint or argument
writingTask.modelAnswer: According to Source B, the Democratic Republic of Congo represents a grim historical paradox rooted not in weakness but in its immense natural wealth. The author explains that foreign powers plundered Congo for centuries, beginning with the 15th-century Portuguese slave trade and continuing through King Leopold of Belgium’s brutal rubber regime. Later, valuable minerals such as copper, uranium, and coltan fueled global world wars and the modern digital revolution, yet the Congolese people remained impoverished, uneducated, and denied the chance to build stable institutions. Following an unprepared independence in 1960, Cold War interference supported dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, whose fall in 1997 triggered devastating conflict involving nine nations. Consequently, the relentless battle to control vast resources turned a natural blessing into a tragic curse of ongoing poverty and instability.
writingTask.compareTip: Review your draft against the checklist: verify that you included source attribution, named specific historical examples and minerals, explained the weakness versus wealth contrast, and stayed within 100–140 words.
